utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we continue to sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis, with Judge Morrison being away, due to his personal matters. Mr. Tieger, do you have a new member today?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We do, Mr. President. And Mr. Olmsted, Matthew Olmsted, will be taking the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Olmsted, welcome on board. Before we continue, there are three matters I'd like to deal with, which are directed to the Defence. First, the Chamber would like to address an issue stemming from the accused's motion to admit testimony of Pero Rendic pursuant to Rule 92 bis, filed on the 8th of January, 2014. In the motion, the accused submits that he had planned to call this witness to testify on the 16th of February [sic], 2014, but that the witness indicated that he was unable and unwilling to testify due to a heart condition. The witness was listed as a 92 ter witness on the revised witness list and the Rule 92 ter notification pertaining to him was filed on 17th December, 2013, with reference to the transcript of his testimony from the Kvocka et al case in 2001, and no reference to the fact that he was unable to testify. It is therefore unclear to the Chamber from the information provided in the motion when the witness's condition came to be known to the accused and his Defence team. Mr. Robinson, could you look into this and get back to the Chamber either orally or in writing before the end of this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the next two matters, could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless there's further administrative matters to be dealt with, we'll bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. For the record, would the counsel assisting Mr. Stanisic introduce himself, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Slobodan Zecevic. I'm counsel assisting Mr. Stanisic, and I'm assisted, with the leave of the Trial Chamber, with Ms. Ibna Catalina Fajardo Rodriguez at my side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning to you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would have a short submission before we start, with the leave of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honours, Mico Stanisic is here to testify not on his free will, as you know, but as he was ordered by this Trial Chamber to -- which ordered him to testify by subpoena. Defence recalls the paragraph 15 of the decision to subpoena Mico Stanisic where the Trial Chamber specifically stated that it maintains its discretion under Rule 90(E) to compel or not compel a witness to answer certain questions. In exercising this discretion it will be cognizant of the fact that Stanisic is currently involved in appeal proceedings at the Tribunal and will ensure that his rights are safe-guarded. Defence understands this statement in light of the Appeals Chamber decision in relation to Tolimir subpoena, paragraphs 44 and 45, where Appeals Chamber specifically emphasised that any self-incriminating testimony inadvertently provided during Mico Stanisic's testimony in Karadzic case could not be used directly or indirectly against him and that the Prosecution would be prohibited from attempting to tender into evidence on appeal any self-incriminating information derived from Stanisic testimony or any evidence derived therefrom. We, therefore, Your Honours, read it to mean that the Rule 90(E) applies to all of Mico Stanisic testimony, questions and answers. Your Honours, Mico Stanisic will obviously necessarily testify of his acts and conduct and that is exactly what is the core of our appeal where we are using his acts and conduct to establish that he was not a member of the JCE as found in the Trial Chamber judgement. As a practical matter, the Defence respectfully proposes to the Trial Chamber to compel Mr. Stanisic to testify in accordance with Rule 90(E) at this point, whereupon Mr. Stanisic will testify, rather than to have Defence object to each question and/or Mr. Stanisic refuse to answer each and every question. From the aspect of judicial economy and undisturbed proceedings, we respectfully say our request is justified. That was my submission, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before I turn to the parties, Mr. Zecevic, if you could clarify this. What's the distinction as you see them between the subpoena and the compulsion or compelling the witness to testify pursuant to Rule 90(E)? Depending upon the nature of the question? Mr. Stanisic has been already ordered despite notwithstanding his refusal to come to the Court to testify by our decision that subpoena. So Chamber has already ordered him to testify against his will. But do you need additional order to compel him to testify, irrespective of the nature of his answers?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we believe in order to protect the rights of Mr. Stanisic on his appeal, that we would need the Trial Chamber to compel him to testify in accordance with the 90(E) -- Rule 90(E). The thing is, Your Honours, that we -- we assume that the -- that the vast majority of the testimony of Mr. Stanisic will be about his acts and conduct, and as I explained, this is the -- the core issue on our appeal. And that is why we believe that -- that he should be compelled to testify in accordance with 90(E). Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One more question before I turn to the parties. So, we received his statement given -- or tendered to the Defence. So -- so this will not be tendered unless the Chamber orders him to -- to testify pursuant to Rule 90(E)?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Robinson, do you like to make any observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We confirm Mr. Zecevic's understanding with respect to the statement and that was the conditions under which the statement was given that it would not be tendered until or unless he was compelled to answer because the contents of the statement clearly could be -- come within Rule 90(E), and whether the Chamber wishes to compel him to answer on a question-by-question basis or on -- as far as the cross-examination is concerned, or whether it wishes to have a more general decision on that, we -- we leave to the discretion of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you address the issue whether the Chamber needs to order him in vacuum to testify pursuant to Rule 90(E) irrespective of the nature of the question whether it -- whether the answer of -- which incriminates or does not incriminate the accused -- the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, there's two -- if we can break that down into two components: First of all, the direct examination. The first sentence of Rule 90(E) says a witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. So when Dr. Karadzic asks him to confirm that this is his statement and that he would give the same evidence, he has the right to object to making the statement, and I think you would have the decision on -- on a global basis as to whether or not to compel him to make this statement and therefore have it tendered as in lieu of his direct testimony. Moving -- even though there are some parts of that statements such as paragraph 4, "I was born on the 30th of June, 1954," which would not be incriminating but as a whole, the statement is being tendered, so I think it's safe to do it that way, on a global basis for the direct examination. But turning to the cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't follow. So paragraph 4 cannot be used by the Prosecution because it is compelled pursuant to Rule 90(E).

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is that your submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Turning to the cross-examination, I think the fair reading of the Rule would require or suggest that a question-by-question invocation of Rule 90(E) is the better practice. That's our position on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When we discussed as to whether Mr. Stanisic should be led live instead of presenting his evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter, this was not addressed to the Chamber, wasn't it, Mr. Robinson? You didn't raise that this whole statement is -- is tendered pursuant to Rule 90(E) with the understanding that this will be tendered only when he is compelled to testify pursuant Rule 90(E).

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think that was the intention of paragraph 3 of the statement. But perhaps it's not so explicit. But we understood when Mr. Stanisic gave us this statement that he was -- he was invoking Rule 90(E) that nothing in the statement would be considered a waiver of his right pursuant to 90(E) and, as indicated in paragraph 2, we were doing it this way for the purpose of judicial economy, so that we could present his evidence in the most efficient way possible. So I'm sorry if it was not explicitly addressed, but we were of the opinion that this is how we would be doing it pursuant to this paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger or Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Olmsted may have some matters to raise when I complete my submission based on his more intimate understanding of the facts and backdrop related to the specific instance. But let me say a few matters quickly, having been caught a bit by surprise as the Bench has been as well. The first matter I intended to raise was the last one raised by the Court. This issue would have been appropriately raised at the time of the discussion concerning whether or not Mr. Stanisic's testimony should be led live or via the statement. And in that respect, I would also note Mr. Robinson's reference to paragraph 3. I would -- of the statement. I would suggest that it indicates quite the opposite, that -- that Mr. Stanisic -- the indication there in paragraph 3 is that you now have an entire statement but we reserve the right on a case-by-case basis to object. There's certainly no suggestion as we are experiencing now that there's going to be an effort to -- to -- seek compulsion for the submission before the submission of the entire statement. I would also note that we have the statement, a signed statement, and the -- it exists, and there's now a signed statement by this witness that was submitted voluntarily without compulsion that is in the -- physically exists. Everybody knows the provenance. We have that document, attempting to draw some kind of formalistic distinction between the preparation and submission of that statement to the parties and to the Court, and the tendering into evidence serves some purposes, but it doesn't appear to me to be a point for purposing of 90(E), at least with respect to this statement. The statement now exists, has been provided without compulsion and that's one of the significant factors here, especially when Mr. Robinson tries to draw a distinction between the way we should handle cross-examination and the way we should handle examination-in-chief. The cross-examination arises, in our submission, from the issues presented by this statement which was submitted to the parties without invocation to 90(E) with only a reservation that during the course of the proceeding, the witness may, nevertheless, attempt to invoke 90(E) as to some matters unspecified. That means that we have a -- a statement that has been provided in one manner. Now we'll move to cross, which should be handled in exactly the same manner. A witness cannot waive his right to object to a particular item and then on -- on examination-in-chief and provided it into evidence and then shield himself from cross-examination by invoking the privilege against self-incrimination with respect to the same item he's already testified about or provided information about. So that's another problem. Mr. Robinson -- or Mr. Zecevic, I believe, raised the Tolimir decision. I believe he is referring to paragraph 43 or 44 of that decision which referred to Mr. -- how the Court in that particular case would choose to deal with matters that might be elicited during his testimony even if there wasn't a specific invocation of the privilege against self-incrimination. That was very case specific as we read it and had a great deal to do, as the Court seemed to emphasise with the fact that Mr. Tolimir was self-represented. But, in any event, it wasn't a blanket position taken by the Appeals Chamber. I think that much seems to be clear but it did -- it indicated that in certain circumstances the protections would apply not only to matters which were specifically invoked or matters for which there was a specific invocation made but also perhaps to other matters in light, in that instances, in particular, of Mr. Tolimir's self-represented status. So suggesting to the Court that it's a blanket rule I think is somewhat misleading. That also seems to militate in favour of the question-by-question approach that this Court has adopted in related proceedings thus far, and it's -- it's -- while we can see kind of a form of economy in a sort of blanket approach, that's not the cautious approach this Trial Chamber has employed in the past. And finally, I would note that the Court has made a distinction between the subpoena process which brought -- which brings a witness here, and the compulsion process which may take -- may or may not take place after a witness is indeed here, and we saw that in a very recent appearances as the Court is aware. I'm also aware that that's the practice in certain jurisdictions across the globe, not all to be sure but in a number of them, where the jurisprudence makes a distinction between compelling a witness to appear by way of subpoena and then independently addressing the issue of whether or not certain questions give rise to a privilege against self-incrimination. So many issues arise by way of what has just been raised, matters which I believe could have been raised before and contrary to the suggestion that we were somehow put on notice that this matter would be raised, Prosecution submits that a fair reading of the entirety of the circumstances, including the fact that it wasn't raised when it should have been, including the reasonable inference to be drawn from paragraph 3, would suggest the opposite, that this issue is not one that could have been expected had we been properly notified that we would be confronting this particular kind of problem. I believe the Bench and the Prosecution would have undertaken both some specific inquiries and some specific additional research to address the issues raised now. That's about all the assistance I can be at this point, Mr. President. I -- I don't -- I -- I certainly don't think that treating, at this point, given the complexities that have arisen, that treating the statement -- pretending to revert back to a situation that existed prior to the time that this statement was drafted, signed, memorialised, signed, and submitted to the parties is rather unrealistic. And, in any event, I don't believe that dealing with it as a blanket matter, that is failing to distinguish between the clearly non-incriminatory matters that may arise and matters that may give rise to a -- a potentially legitimate invocation of 90(E) will -- will be a productive approach. So I would urge the Court as I think the -- the Court was already leaning to reject the effort to treat this -- to approach this matter as suggested by Mr. Zecevic and Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, would the refusal -- I'm asking you, Mr. Tieger, would the refusal to testify after having been subpoenaed, whether or not the question would incriminate the witness, not constitute a contempt of Tribunal? That's a refusal to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would have to think about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless ordered pursuant to Rule 90(E), whether the question would be incriminating or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I understood. I -- I -- I -- that's a very good point. I -- I -- and I was focussing on the -- the issues raised by subpoenaed witnesses who have already signalled an intention or concern about 90(E). So that was the nature of my response. I -- I tend to think the Court is right. It is simply a blanket refusal to testify after being subpoenaed without resort to any justification. That's essentially -- the -- the Court would be -- would be correct. My focus was on the circumstances we've been facing of late, where the -- we've been delving with potential 90(E) matters, and although the relation -- although as the Court I think noted in one of its decisions, the relationship between the subpoena and the invocation of 90(E) is very close, they're not identical. And, as I say, I'm aware of jurisdictions where that distinction is made. But setting that issue aside, if a witness decided to respond to a subpoena and then showed up and said, Okay, I'm here but there is no way I'm going to co-operate with the Court. I contumaciously refuse to participate in these proceedings without giving any reason, then I presume the Court would be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I turn to you, Mr. Zecevic. Rule 90(E), the first sentence of that provision reads like this: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness." So, therefore, I ask you the same question that I asked

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Irrespective of the question, the nature of the question, whether it incriminates the witness or not, the refusal to testify on the part of the witness, if he is not to -- compelled pursuant to Rule 90(E) would constitute a contempt of the Tribunal, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would -- with all due respect, I disagree. The Rule 90(E) is -- is a provision of the Rules which -- which protects the right of the accused who is compelled to testify -- who is -- who is testifying in the -- in the -- or the witness who is testifying in the proceedings. As the Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber already established, we are here faced with the very specific situation where the -- where the -- where the -- whereas witnesses, we have the persons who are in the process -- or, rather, different stages of the process before this Tribunal. In this case, is the appeal of Mico Stanisic. And, therefore, his concerns are, I believe, legitimate. Mr. Stanisic does not - and I repeat, does not - does not refuse to testify. He came here on the subpoena order of this Trial Chamber. He provided the -- the statement. So, therefore, obviously Mr. Stanisic would like to assist the Trial Chamber. The issue here is the protection of his right which we believe can only be protected by -- by the Rule 90(E). The nature of the -- of his testimony, I -- I emphasise again, is such that it would -- it would necessarily in a majority or in the bigger part refer to his acts and conduct. And, as I say, that is the core issue on his appeal. And therefore we -- we suggested as a practical matter that the Trial Chamber compels him to testify and, therefore, we can -- we can continue with -- with the testimony of Mico Stanisic as -- as -- as planned. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one question for you, Mr. Zecevic. By way of example, his background, paragraphs 4 to 12. Take paragraph 4, "I was born in 30th June, 1954, in Pale municipality." Would he not testify unless compelled pursuant to Rule 90(E) about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, he would, Your Honours. This is -- this is just the preliminary -- his background information which is in no dispute whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So when you referred to his acts and conduct, what did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have in mind the -- the acts and conduct in the relevant time of his indictment and the judgement which was -- which was handed in his case on the 27 March of last year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless there are any matters to address, the Chamber -- the Chamber will rise for about a half-hour to consider this issue. --- Break taken at 9.40 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having heard the submissions of the parties and counsel for Mr. Mico Stanisic, and also having reviewed the proposed Rule 92 ter statement, the Chamber is not satisfied that the protection of Rule 90(E) can apply for the entirety of the statement. The Chamber is, therefore, of the view that Mr. Stanisic should be led live. This will allow the witness to invoke the protection of Rule 90(E) for each question posed that may tend to incriminate him. That's the ruling. And, Mr. Karadzic, you may proceed. But before that, I'd like to give Mr. Stanisic an advice as to his right pursuant to Rule 90(E). As you may know well, Mr. Stanisic, I must draw your attention to that Rule. That is, Rule 90(E). Under this Rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges, if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence, or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But, in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency. Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to all. Examination by Mr. Karadzic

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Minister.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I see that you already have experience with pausing, and I kindly ask you to caution me as well. There should be a pause between questions and answers, and also we should speak slowly so that everything could be recorded in the transcript. Since the statement is not being admitted, I will have to put a few general questions to you so that they could be recorded. Could you give us your full name and surname and your place and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: My name is Mico Stanisic. I was born on the 30th of June, 1954, in the municipality of Pale, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us briefly about your education.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I completed elementary school in my place of birth, secondary school in Sarajevo, and I graduated from the University of Sarajevo; I have a degree in law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you also tell us about your professional career before 1990, because we will be dealing with that specifically. What did you do in which period of time?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: From 1973 until the end of 1984, I worked at the city SUP, the SUP of the city of Sarajevo in Bosnia-Herzegovina. From 1984 until 1991, I worked in business. Again, from May 1991, I worked as the secretary of the city SUP. And then from February 1992 until the beginning of the war, I worked in the republican SUP as an advisor to the minister. And then from April 1994 -- or, actually, 1992, I worked as minister of the MUP of the Serbia Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that your only involvement in the MUP of Republika Srpska in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: No. From January 1994 until the end of July 1994, again, I was minister in the MUP of Republika Srpska, and thereby I concluded my activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether you and I knew each other before 1990, and also could you tell us how it was that you got involved in the preparations for establishing a democratic party in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: We did not know each other personally before 1990, although I knew your name. Actually, sometime in mid-1984, there were some proceedings, I think it had to do with some misdemeanour in the economic sector, and I was attached to my colleagues from the city SUP who were -- who dealt with white-collar crime. I just prepared in terms of preparing documents from a company which was called Gradinski Energoinvest from Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I have a correction in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It said "misdemeanour in academic sector" and now it's changed to "economic sector." I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the outcome was of these proceedings before this court of law?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know the final judgement was one of acquittal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now tell us about your meetings with persons who worked on the establishment of the party in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: In 1990, I think his name was Jovan Ilik [phoen]. He worked for Neoplanta from Novi Sad. So we had this co-operation in the business sector and he told me that the democratic party was to be established and he mentioned the names of certain professors, renowned professors, and he said that the statute had to be worked out for that party, and since I had a degree in law, I accepted. I said I would help in terms of preparing the statute for the democratic party of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember what our relations were with Micunovic's democratic party, and did you attend the founding assembly and was Micunovic present at the founding assembly?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I think his name was Galic - I cannot remember exactly - from Micunovic's democratic party. He is the person who helped with the statute because the intention was to have these two parties be identical. And Micunovic was present at the promotion event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the position of Micunovic's party in Serbia at the time? Was it in power? Was it an opposition party?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: At that time there was just one party that was in power because this was still the Communist system and that was the socialist party, actually, the Communist party of Yugoslavia. The democratic party that was established then was an opposition party and, of course, the Communist party viewed it not exactly with satisfaction. Sorry, can I just add something. The democratic party brought together the high "inteligencija," intellectuals, in terms of its activity and its very establishment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Our adoption of the name the Serbian, et cetera, did you see any reason for that in terms of the other political organisations of the other two peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give a precise answer as to why -- well, I can speculate but then why the name was changed in the Serb Democratic Party. This was done just before the promotion event for establishing the party. And I know that in Bosnia-Herzegovina two national parties has already been established, the SDA and the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us, after the elections, were you on some list of ours for the elections?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: No. No. I was just on the initiative committee for the establishment of the democratic party. At that time, as far as I was informed, it was supposed to be professor, Dr. Kecmanovic, who was supposed to be head of that party. However, at the event itself there were certain changes. I think that Professor Kecmanovic took over the reformist party of Ante Markovic in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were not on the election lists. Can you tell us, after the elections and after the election victory, how did your professional career evolve? What happened in 1991 after the joint government was established of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: After this promotion event which took place at Skenderija, since I had enrolled in a graduate course at the University of Belgrade, my realistic assessment was that I am not really one for politics, that I should stick to my profession. So that's why I left all of this together and started working on scholarly matters, in addition to my professional work in the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point in time, were you asked to fill one of the positions that the Serb community got in the joint organs?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: At the very outset, when posts were being filled, I was not supposed to be involved in any way. It was only later in May 1991, or the beginning of 1991, I don't really want to engage in guess-work now, there was a vacancy, the secretary of the SUP of Sarajevo, and the then-officials of the republican MUP, Momcilo Mandic and Vitomir Zepinic, since they knew me as a person who had dedicated his entire life to his tasks and work at the Ministry of the Interior, and after all special schools are completed to that end, then he -- they came and asked me to become involved in this, and they said that they had consent to do this. This was the beginning of 1991, the month of May, and I accepted that, and Alija Delimustafic appointed me to that position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber to the best of your knowledge whether these two top people in the MUP, on behalf of the Serbs, whether they were members of the SDS, and did the party give full freedom to professionals to appoint their own people, or was it the political party that made these appointments on the basis of party membership and affiliation?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: This is what Momcilo Mandic and Vitomir Zepinic said to me: These official positions were not allocated in terms of political parties, the SDS or the HDZ or, rather, these people who represent the people would choose personnel to work with them, so they chose people who would work in their line of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me what the situation was with other appointments in the MUP, what your experience is, what you know, what was the guiding principle there? Party affiliations or professionalism?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, for the most part of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer. Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I could have raised this objection to the earlier questions, but this is extremely leading on the issue of party membership and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. If -- Mr. Stanisic, if you could answer the question whether these appointments in the MUP was operated under what principle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that in the MUP the main principle was professionalism; that is to say, people who were of professional integrity for carrying out these tasks and duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us something about the other two communities? How did they relate to that principle?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: How should I put it? I can speak in general terms rather than in details because I didn't dwell much upon it. I do know, however, that many members of the Ministry of the Interior arrived without having ever performed such tasks in the past. And they had been sent by the SDA and the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us what was the nature of our contacts. Did we have any private contact of any kind?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: We never had any kind of private contact. We were in touch regarding the party but seldom. You worked together with the professors on the various political matters and you did not deal with the statute. There was a working group set up for that purpose. I worked in it but not for long because the statute was drafted by Mr. Gajic from Belgrade and we simply adjusted it to the conditions in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As regards such contacts, once you had assumed your duties in the MUP what was the nature of our contact? Did you call me? Did I call you? And what was the topic of our discussions? What was the need which dictated that contact?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: If we take into account the length of time I spent with the MUP and the number of our contacts, the number was minimal. It mainly had to do with tasks related to security in the area of the city of Sarajevo, such as providing security for persons, facilities, yourself, et cetera. It -- this involved all such people who were supposed to be guarded by the SUP Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I haven't finished. I only know that our contact was infrequent but I don't remember who called who.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the appointment of Serb personnel in the MUP, was this done according to a pre-arranged plan and did it go smoothly? Was -- did I call the MUP in that regard, or did the MUP revert to me?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: It was mainly Momcilo Mandic and Vitomir Zepinic who dealt with it. I do know, however, that when we met, they stated such problems to be existing. The biggest problem was the position of deputy chief of state security which was supposed to be someone from the SUP in Sarajevo. According to the arrangement between the three parties, a Serb was supposed to be appointed to that position but the process was never completed. Ultimately, pressure was exerted to fill that vacancy and for that person to be Serb. The solution applied was dealt by the SDA and the HDZ --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly repeat the names of the two people mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And finally the post was abolished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, could you kindly repeat the names of two individuals.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The two people responsible for the abolishment of the post were the minister, Alija Delimustafic, and the chief State Security Service, Branislav Kvesic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kvesic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are still in the pre-war period. Minister, tell us what was your understanding of my position vis-a-vis interethnic relations, and what was your position regarding the same topic? Did you notice anything regarding my position and my opinion of the other ethnic communities that you would disapprove of?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would need to object at this point and ask that the witness be compelled to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it would make it easier if the question was -- there's quite a few questions in there. But I think the real question was the first one. So it might be easier for the Chamber in deciding on this issue if Dr. Karadzic just rephrased his question and asked about his own -- about Dr. Karadzic's views on this topic without asking about the witness's position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, in that case, we'll hear Mr. Karadzic's revised question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. I was trying to save time but it turned out I actually spent more of it this way. Minister, before the conflict broke out, were you familiar with my position regarding the ethnic communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina and, in your view, what was my position?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, after such a long time, I can only speak in general terms. I know what you generally stood for, and I believe, first and foremost, you were in favour of preserving Yugoslavia. Later on, you proposed that the ethnic issue be dealt with on the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as regards the Serbs, without infringing upon the area or rights of the other two peoples. I do know that there was an international commission tasked with dealing with this issue, and I based my position on their views. Politically speaking, there were different views on different sides, and they did not agree ultimately on what might have been possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you observe any discrimination or intolerance on my part regarding the other two ethnic communities?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: To the extent of my knowledge at the time, I could not conclude that you were in favour of interethnic conflict but, rather, a political solution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Minister, before the war and during the war, were you free to voice your position and did I or someone else try to impose anything? Did you have to come in conflict with people for putting your position fort?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Could you be more specific in terms of period? You mentioned before and during the war ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please put a pause between the question and answer. Do you understand that, Mr. Stanisic? On your part as well, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I could go back. You said before the war, Zepinic and Mandic were in contact with me more frequently than you. In any case, during that period, as a member of the collegium, were you free to speak and were you ever in conflict with me for speaking your mind?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I always spoke clearly and freely. No one could put pressure on me to say something I did not want.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did I hold it against you? Did you have any trouble with me for speaking freely? And did you have trouble with anyone else for doing that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, it's leading. Mr. Karadzic should simply ask how he responded to this rather than suggesting answers for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, probably you can reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was my position regarding your professional autonomy, when it came to speaking the truth?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Kindly be more precise. When?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war, although you were in contact more with some other MUP personnel, as well as during the war. Did I hold it against you? What was my position regarding your professional integrity?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: During the war, we were only in official contact by way of my reports and if you asked for any clarification, but it happened seldom. When I put forth requests to the Presidency, such as, for instance, the issue of engaging the Presidency in dealing with problems which fell outside the scope of authority of the Ministry of the Interior but had consequences which had to be addressed simultaneously by the MUP and other bodies, I would receive a positive response from you, but would encounter obstacles from some other Presidency members, as well as the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you recall whether in early March 1992 -- well, what position did you hold at the time? And can you tell us something more about the reasons why and the process of setting up barricades in and around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think it was on the 1st of March that the barricades began being set up in Sarajevo as a reaction which followed the killing of a wedding party member in front of the old church in the old town of Sarajevo. When the news was broadcast, barricades were set up; on one side there were Serbs and on the other were Muslims. At the time I was minister's advisor in charge of national security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were we in communication then and what were our respective positions in order to deal with the crisis?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I think we were in telephone contact. Members of the BiH MUP who were Serbs and Muslim, received tasking from the minister to use their influence with their respective communities to have the barricades removed in order to secure normal functioning of the city. It took place on the 2nd of March, because we were all taken by surprise when the barricades were set up on the 1st of March. So the MUP engagements began on March 2 in order to remove the barricades. I think it was on the 2nd of March that we spoke by telephone. You were interested in removing the barricades. But in order for us not to create any further problems, we wanted to do it in a peaceful way. The result of our engagement was that, indeed, the barricades were removed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly see P5602. It is an intercept of our telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First, I spoke to Jovo Jovanovic. Can you remind the Chamber who he was?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Jovo Jovanovic was the president of the town board of the SDS, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Towards the bottom, I asked him what was it like in the town. Do you know where I -- I was on the 1st and 2nd of March?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I really don't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 5 in the Serbian and 6 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll read out my response and yours: "Radovan Karadzic: How come they are not ashamed to kill someone at a wedding ceremony? That's utterly insane. It is probably because nobody could have stopped those Serbs. Will you be able to persuade the people to remove barricades?" Your answer: "Listen, now we are a little ... I mean, I have just commented it here. We have to do it gradually. That's because their forces have almost covered this check-point here in Pofalici." Further down you say: "They have it covered by snipers." And then even further down you say: "Conditions have been met for both to withdraw from the barricades." It was your response.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in the Serbian and page 7 in the English. Yes, that's where we have this last reply that the conditions have been met. Now we need page 6 in Serbian and 8 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is where I say: "The bilateral dismantling of barricades should be at midnight." You say: "Exactly." And so on and so forth. Everybody can read this. What was the position? Was there a concordance of opinion with this regard between you and me?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: First of all, president, Mr. Karadzic as regards the first part, I'd like to say that I had received the task from Momcilo Mandic to talk to Jovo Jovanovic, who was the president of the SDS in the town of Sarajevo. He was supposed to deal with the situation from his party position. Momcilo Mandic was supposed to talk to Rajko Djukic, who was the president of the Executive Board of the party. The Muslim side also received the task to talk to their officials. I did what I was supposed to do. It is true that fire was opened from sniper, and I believe that the Muslim side even... there was a casualty at the Pofalici check-point. One lad died. He lived close to that check-point. His name was Strajo Pandurevic. We carried out an on-site investigation, hence we were aware of the details. It is true that he also insisted that everything should be done peacefully. I carried out my task as far as I could together with my other colleagues who were engaged and that was done to the satisfaction of everybody in the town of Sarajevo. The barricades on both sides were dismantled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnic background of the casualty at the barricade?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Minister, were you aware of the negotiations about the transformation of Bosnia? And in view of the fact that you were an advisor in the MUP, were you involved in the first Council of Ministers of the Serbian entity?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a portfolio at the time?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. My involvement was a result -- or, rather, this is when -- what I was told. Vitomir Zepinic was appointed as the minister of the interior. And at the time, information leaked about some dodgy deals on his behalf and one of the MPs didn't want him to be minister so somebody proposed a comprise and said, Let there be another person from the MUP. I believe the MP who reacted was from Doboj and he was the one who proposed my name. I was a minister without portfolio therefore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you among the most important people in the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: No. I believe that there was nearly nobody from the SDS. I don't know how many members there were but over 60 per cent of them were not SDS members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please now tell us whether you were familiar with our negotiations with Cutileiro. What results did we achieve, especially with regard to the existence of the police forces of the future entities of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I believe that every single citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina was familiar with the negotiations. They followed in anticipation as to what would happen because the federal state had disintegrated, the position of Bosnia-Herzegovina was not known at the time, so we were obviously all very interested in our lot. The solutions offered by Cutileiro at that moment were accepted by a majority of the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, me included.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What led to the setting up of the Serbian MUP -- or, rather, the two MUPs? How is that accepted on both sides initially and what happened later? But let's take things one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes, can we take things one at a time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking about our reasons for requesting that from Cutileiro but, rather, what was the basis of the setting up of the two MUPs?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: The constitutional solutions for Bosnia-Herzegovina were adopted by all the three sides in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was envisaged that Bosnia would remain an independent state, that it would consist of three entities, the Serbian, Croat, and Muslim entities, and that the entities should also have their own police forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And now can you tell us when was the MUP divided and how you parted?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: That was after the signing of Cutileiro's plan. There are minutes from the collegium of the MUP, when it was agreed that the transformation of MUP rather than the division of MUP should be carried out in keeping with the constitutional provisions offered by Cutileiro's plan and that this should be done peacefully; that all the members should be protected; that it should be left to the will of all the members of the MUP as to where they would go on working, in which body, and that the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina should remain as the umbrella institution that would be above all the entity MUPS; that the communication system should remain the same because that was important. Up to then, everything was located at the level of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the Dayton Accords? How did the Dayton deal with the issue of police forces?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I believe that the solutions were identical. There may have been some aberrations, but more or less the situation was identical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What were you offered? What position were you offered after the transformation of the MUP into two different MUPs?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I believe that Prime Minister Djeric defined it in the best possible way. He was the one who proposed me as a minister. We had had long talks about that. At first I refused the position, obviously. But then he kept on persuading me and trying to convince me that a reasonable man cannot understand that after the Cutileiro Plan and after the solutions to the crisis in Croatia and the presence of the United Nations in Sarajevo, i.e., in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that there could be conflicts of any kind and that each of us individuals had their jobs to do, because that was normal and our position. And after all that, he convinced me to accept the position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Initial -- were you in a position to present your views as to how you regarded the police of the Serbian entity?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: At the assembly meeting, I wanted the MPs to hear my views of the MUP, so I told them very precisely in -- in no uncertain terms as to what was my vision of the MUP of Republika Srpska was and what its obligations were supposed to be, and you can see it in the minutes because my speech was recorded. It was supposed to be the MUP that would be professional, that would be engaged in the policing tasks envisaged by the law, which was the framework of it -- its work and nothing else but that. And that should have been done without any discrimination and all the citizens in Republika Srpska should have enjoyed an equal treatment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown 1D9510. We're going to display the transcript. We can also listen to the audio recording, if necessary. The sound on the video is not very good. That's why we are actually offering the transcript. Could we also be provided with the Serbian version of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Minister, could you please tell us something about your intervention in the last paragraph after you were given the floor. Was that your first address in the new position?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Could you give me a moment to read the passage? Yes, these are, indeed, my words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When it comes to the police and the politics, did they accept your professional attitude towards work?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, they adopted President Djeric's proposal which means that they accepted my views with regard to the makeup of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned legality is based on the negotiations of the three ethnic entities under the auspices of the European community. Is this what we referred to as Cutileiro Plan?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the only reason why I accepted the position. Without that I would never have accepted it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document please be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4271, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any difficulty with admitting the video in -- together with this transcript, Mr. Olmsted?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it in its entirety, as well as the video.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us something about the 30th of March. At the beginning of April, did you still meet with your colleagues from the Muslim and Croat MUP?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: After this collegium meeting, I did have talks with Jusuf Pusina. It was at his own initiative. I agreed very gladly because he had been chosen by Alija Izetbegovic, who was the president of the SDA, to negotiate with me in order to deal with the transformation process, without any hiccups. We met on the 3rd of April, I believe. It was in Grbavica in a bar or in a pizza parlor. We discussed the matters there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was agreed with regard to the headquarters of the Serbian MUP? And the Croat and Muslim MUP, where were those supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I have to be very precise and tell you what was agreed at that time. We agreed everything but the headquarters of the future MUPs. Jusuf Pusina told me during that meeting that he could not say anything without an additional consultation with President Izetbegovic. We agreed to meet again on the 5th of April, 1992. However, in the meantime, there were parallel talks about that between Momcilo Mandic and Minister Alija Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was an agreement reached with regard to the headquarters of the Serbian special police?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: This is what I know: Momcilo Mandic and Alija Delimustafic, who was minister at the time, agreed that temporarily within the complex of the school for policemen in Vrace, which was the previous headquarters of the special brigade of Bosnia and Herzegovina which had moved to Krtelj in Ilidza, the MUP of Croatia -- Croatia -- of Republika Srpska and its special should be billeted there, that that should be their headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the MUP and the specials of Republika Srpska really occupy that facility and what happened?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I was not involved in that. I didn't know much about that, to be honest. I didn't even know about the agreement which was reached between Alija and Momcilo Mandic. However, subsequently I learned that -- what Mandic and Alija had agreed and that as a result of that agreement, Momcilo Mandic invited that part of the special brigade to move to that facility in Vrace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when the Serbian specials arrived in Vrace, according to what you subsequently learnt?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I learned what had happened, obviously. To -- I can't give you any precise details. However, the -- there was a training for police members who were armed in that same facility. They carried dangerous weapons, and when that part of the brigade and members of the Serbian ethnicity arrived in the facility, fire was opened on them, and two members of the brigade were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And how was that first conflict resolved? Were there any casualties on the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: No, there weren't. That part of the special brigade reached the facility, but there was heavy fighting that took them by surprise. But they had all been given orders not to open fire at anybody, despite the fact that fire may have been opened on them. The reason was to prevent further escalation of the problem. There were two casualties. Nobody was wounded on the their side, but they did capture those who had opened fire on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As noted, we'll take a short break for 15 minutes and resume at 11.30. --- Break taken at 11.16 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Minister, could you please tell us whether you remember how many persons did the members of the Serb special forces take prisoner on that day at Vrace, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I cannot really exactly. I cannot remember the exact number. But I know that when they disarmed that group that had done this, they kept them within the school compound in Vrace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to them soon after that?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: They went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the media in Sarajevo? How did they portray this thing that happened in Vrace? "Incident" is not a word that would be strong enough.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, of course, I mean, the media were used for propaganda at the time, rather than for conveying the truth. I really cannot recall any details now, but I do know that I reacted by way of a letter to this propaganda. The result of all this incorrect information could have been causing fear among people, so I felt duty-bound to send this letter to inform the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina about what had actually happened, irrespective of whose fault it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you ask to have this made public?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Bosnia Radio Television.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 05287 in e-court; that's the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, could you please zoom in a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the letter that you spoke about, the 18th of April; right?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Could I just see the last page, the signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the second page or, rather, third page? Because there are some empty pages there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is my signature. Yes, that's the letter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we stay on page 2. For the participants, it's also page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you the following --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, could you go back to that page with the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One-sided and unverified information that are being put into the public domain on the basis of reports by citizens from one source only, only contribute to an escalation of the war conflict. And further on, you say that that is not useful for anyone or anything. Also, you resolutely deny the news that the Serb forces fired at the RTS building, et cetera. Do you remember this letter?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't want to pour more oil on the fire, as they say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this letter please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Olmsted?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4272, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Minister, I believe that you know that you are mentioned in the indictment, in my indictment, as some kind of co-member, co-perpetrator of mine in a joint criminal enterprise, aimed at removing Muslims and Croats from the territories that we believed we had a right to, that we had obtained that we believed that we were entitled to. Could you tell me, first of all, from the point of view of the MUP, the joint MUP and the transformed MUP, the Serb MUP and the Serb police, did they have any plans that would confirm these assertions made in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: There are two questions. First, the one up here, whether I had this joint objective with you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry. I need to object because, first of all, there are two questions. And the first one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we deal -- deal with it one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic, put your question again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me not ask you. Your answer was that we had no personal relations, that we were not friends. Formally, were you a member of some joint criminal enterprise together with me? Anything illegal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I hear from you, Mr. Olmsted, first.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just a very leading questions, Your Honours. Of course it goes to the legal conclusion as well, his membership in a joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Leading in light of his comment before that, or the request itself is a leading question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm just reading the question before it. Yes, I mean, it's in conjunction with the question -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please, I don't follow your question. Formally, unformally -- oh, yes. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you would allow that question, I would object to it, and ask that you compel the witness to testify -- to answer that question, sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wanted to check whether it's a translation issue. Line 17, did you ask whether witness was a member of some joint criminal enterprise formally? Or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it's maybe better if he just puts his question with some more simple, less legal language. I think if he can reformulate it, then it would solve most of these problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Minister, you and I, did we have some joint plan or some understanding aimed at expelling Muslims and Croats -- and/or Croats, from territories that we believed we were entitled to?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the position was of your co-workers and your subordinates in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I know what my position was and I can present it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I was just a man who held the post of minister, who did his job exclusively within the framework that was allowed to him by the ministry -- by the Law on the Ministry of the Interior and other laws of the former SFRY because I was convinced that they were not discriminatory in any way. The former Yugoslavia was a signatory of all international conventions and covenants and it had built all of that into its own legislation, and that is how I behaved throughout.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can that be seen from some documents?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: That can be seen from my very first statement that I gave before the Assembly and then all the way up until the end of my tenure as minister at the end of 1992 and those six months in 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown P01096 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us about this? This is information about some aspects of the work done to date and the tasks ahead; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe -- actually, there's something handwritten here that it was submitted to me and ...

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: The prime minister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, the premier. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 4 in Serbian now, and page 3 in English. Could we have the next page in Serbian, please. English, 3; Serbian, 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This paragraph here where it says: "It was pointed out that the priority for both the national service and the crime investigation service is to detect war crimes, provide documentation (on-site investigations, photos, expert testimonies, medical findings) and file criminal reports. Documents are also provided for war crimes committed by Serbs." Can you tell us whether this was actually accepted, whether people worked on this basis, and what was done once a criminal report was filed? What the role of the MUP was after that?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Our tasks - that is to say, the tasks of the members of the Ministry of the Interior - are clearly defined. In accordance with that, I issued an order; namely, that everything that was done necessarily within the scope of our duties was to prevent war crimes, and if this kind of thing did happen, then very seriously all evidence should be collected and everything should be done, all the measures mentioned here. Because evidence is the basis for any kinds of indictment for perpetrators of crimes, that's why I insisted on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Once a criminal report is filed and once it is submitted to the judiciary, can the MUP or anyone else hush things up?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Viewed very specifically, the powers of the prosecutor, the judge, and the Ministry of the Interior, in more complex cases, robbery, murder, war crimes, an investigating judge would have to carry out the on-site investigation. Whereas, the Ministry of the Interior provides technical support and these people who are experts in carrying out all the things that are involved. The Ministry of the Interior can later only act on the basis of the prosecutor, who then takes over. And then if the prosecutor or investigating judge decides to take further action, then that is done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I have the intervention in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe part of the answer was not entered. Perhaps the witness and the -- Mr. Karadzic should be, again, notified to -- to -- to take it slowly because I understand that interpreters are not able to -- to translate all of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell us what is missing from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What is missing is that that -- that -- the part of the testimony where -- where witness talks about who is in charge of preparing the -- the document, the report of the on-site -- on-site investigation, and what is done after such a report is prepared. That was the -- that was the part of the -- the sentence after the sentence which was -- which ended on the -- on -- page 44, line 1. Which ends that -- things that are involved. After that, the part of the answer was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you follow Mr. Zecevic's intervention? Could you repeat that part of your answer, Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. So, once it is established that a crime was carried out, especially a serious crime, then no one can take any action without an investigating judge. An on-site investigation can only be carried out by an investigative judge and he is in charge of the on-site investigation. Assistance can be provided only by members of the Ministry of the Interior from specialised services, the technical service providing expertise in terms of evidence, and so on. Once the on-site investigation is over, then the investigating judge compiles a record of the on-site investigation, a report, and submits it to the prosecutor. Then -- then they carry out an investigation, and the Ministry of the Interior can act only on the basis of their requests, if any, in terms of collecting additional evidence, bringing in a certain witness, and so on. However, they cannot influence the course of the investigation because the judiciary is separate from the executive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I still don't follow what was missing from the transcript. You referred -- it refers to a investigating judge's function. But we'll continue, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. This is precisely what was not recorded. Who prepares the -- the -- the on-site investigation and report and whom it is delivered. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would like you to take a look at lines 21 to 24 of page 43. We shall continue. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, you do not have access to the LiveNote?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid not. I just have -- I have it on the -- on the -- on the monitor over here. I cannot control or go back. That is the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I wanted to tell you, Mr. Zecevic, if necessary, you may ask Mr. Harvey to show him the transcript page that has been already scrolled over, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand, Your Honours. I -- I did apologise for that and ask Mr. Karadzic whether -- whether I'm confusing him by -- by -- by making comments on the transcript, but he -- he told me that it is completely okay, and that they, being very busy, are not able to control the transcript. So that is why I am doing this. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very much appreciated. Thank you. And I take it that would not cause much difficulty on your part, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Of course, not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Mr. Zecevic for assistance with the transcript. [Interpretation] Please go to page 8 in the Serbian and 5 in the English, please. The next page in Serbian. It's probably page eight in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Minister, please look at the last paragraph. There, you enumerate the tasks. You insist on preventing and discovering the perpetrators of serious crimes especially in terms of serious crime against life and limb, et cetera, irrespective of who the perpetrators are. Is that something that was carried out during your tenure and was it accepted by your subordinates in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, does he confirm what is written here? That's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. My only concern here is rather than putting a question to the witness, Mr. Karadzic is simply reading part of a document and asking him to confirm it. And that is leading by its very nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Another piece of advice from a new members, Mr. Karadzic. Bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It was my impression that I had laid a foundation with my first question about the position of the ministry, and now I was just seeking to offer examples corroborating it. But in any case, I can put my question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
