utterances.text: What was the position vis-a-vis and the treatment of war crimes as part of the ministry strategy, the minister of the interior, that is?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: It was clear and unambiguous. War crimes are the gravest crimes which needed to be prevented and perpetrators identified. One must understand that the conditions under which the MUP operated were more than the worse possible, and, if necessary, I can explain. It was for those reasons that we were aware that not all of the measures could be undertaken in such conditions. However, we set apart and insisted that such measures be carried out at least to gather a minimum of evidence in case of such crimes which could serve as a good basis for further processing and in order to have such crimes sanctioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to point out it is on page 6 in the English and 9 in the Serbian where that very point is discussed. You mentioned the conditions. Once the war broke out, where was the seat of the ministry and what kind of equipment, personnel, communications did it have at its disposal as well as premises?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I don't think that any ministry of the interior in the world ever functioned under such conditions. When I say that, I'm trying to say that there wasn't even a minimum of preconditions required to carry out the basic functions of the ministry. Even under such conditions, me and my associates, of whom there were very few, tried to deal with these issues. We put maximum effort humanly possible to tackle such issues. If necessary, since you put the question of where the seat of the ministry was, perhaps I can just tell the Chamber that for the seven months in 1992, the seat of the ministry moved four times. First, it was at Vrace near Sarajevo, then on mount Jahorina, then in Pale, and ultimately in Bijeljina, without water, electricity, communications system. You can just imagine how a ministry can operate under such conditions, if there's only a single telephone line, which is also controlled by the other side. They could interrupt our communication whenever they wanted. We tried from one day to the next to improve it, but there was an additional problem. That being that, especially at first, there was combat interrupting communications and there was no physical contact with the Security Services Centres and security service stations. As that was being dealt with, we tried to set up a better system so as to satisfy at least the minimum of our needs. You'll probably see there is a document where I request a fax machine to be installed in public security stations and centres so that we could have any kind of communication whatsoever. Even that was very difficult to do. I'm saying this only to illustrate what the conditions were like. Also we lacked technical equipment, vehicles, fuel, personnel, both quality-wise and in terms of numbers. In the seat of the ministry, we had a number of secretaries and drivers, and the entire ministry logistics was carried out by less than 20 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As per establishment, how many people should a ministry have, having all these administrations?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Karadzic, 15 people, so it's -- it's a team. It doesn't even suffice for a defence team, let alone a ministry, which covers such a large area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Concerning the police personnel and their profiles, did you have sufficient numbers of personnel and was personnel also engaged in combat? If so, what was the legal basis for it?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: As we can see in the reports, clearly, that in 1992, over 50 per cent of MUP members, i.e., policemen, were engaged in combat activities, based on the principle of resubordination to the military units, which so required. You were the Supreme Commander, and you are far more knowledgeable in terms of which areas necessitated that. The legal basis was the Law on All People's Defence. Under the law of the former Yugoslavia, everyone once -- once there is a state of imminent threat of war, all men of certain age between 8 [as interpreted] and 65 are duty-bound and expected to defend the country, if so required. In the ministries, we performed our work obligations in the execution of our respective duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How did that affect regular policing? Were they engaged in combat all the time, or only in cases of offensives, when it comes to the policemen being sent to theatres of war?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, to the most -- most extent, the answer is yes. We also had a problem with the number of security centres and police stations which were established outside the scope of the Law on the Interior, established by unauthorised personnel and bodies. At that moment there were only war police stations functioning or serving the interests of such organs which tried to provide security in the -- their respective areas. So, they were outside the scope and competence of the Ministry and the Law on the Interior and they had personnel that had not been trained. There were no necessary conditions set in place in order for someone to become a member of the MUP in the first place. Ultimately, these were the people we had many problems with, until we disbanded such bodies. I submitted requests to the -- to you to have such police force disbanded as well as such police stations disbanded so as to enable the ministry to establish some kind of control over them. Orders were issued there, personnel appointed, and financing provided for the functions of such stations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Minister, can you tell us how long one needs to be trained or educated to be a qualified policeman?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: In keeping with the Law on Interior, one could be employed by the MUP in two ways when it comes to policemen. One way was to go through the centre in charge of training and educating personnel for the affairs of the Ministry of the Interior; i.e., once one has completed that kind of education which lasted for four years, there was a -- a period of internship and then the minister could deploy such people, according to their profiles, to various duties in the ministry. The other way was if such training centres were insufficient in terms of numbers of people they provided, separate courses, training courses, were set up by the ministry. Those who could apply had to have a high school diploma and had to meet certain general and special requirements to be employed by the ministry. Those requirements were well defined. One had to undergo a medical check --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: One had to undergo a medical check so that person had to be healthy in every way. Then one also had to come up with certificates from registers of the Ministry of the Interior testifying that they had not previously been prosecuted, convicted, and they had no criminal record. Once those conditions were met, they could be admitted to the Ministry of the Interior and had to undergo a six-month course which had to do with police affairs. And then again, they had to undergo an internship in different organisational units of the Ministry of the Interior. Only once that was done the minister issued decisions on their assignment to different tasks and units.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript, page 51, line 24 and 25, they had to provide testimony that they were not the subject of any criminal investigations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The certificate had to certify that no criminal proceedings were instituted against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Minister. Did you issue instructions to the personnel of the stations and their chiefs, in order to monitor the conduct of their policemen?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Are we still discussing employing personnel or are we already discussing their performance?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: The instructions of what I have discussed are contained in the Law on the Interior and the by-laws and rules on the internal organisation and structure of tasks and duties in the Ministry of the Interior. The rules were under the competence of the government. It was the government who effected them. We applied the rule on internal organisation as we had inherited it from the former Bosnia-Herzegovina until such time when we drafted our own. I cautioned via my orders because a minister can send orders and instructions how they can employ someone to perform tasks and duties in the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness D01671.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is dated 17th of April, one of your earliest issuances. Do you recall it? And how does it fit in with what you have just described? Did you issue this so early in your office?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at the question. You either change your question -- this is my document, but this is not about the hiring but, rather, dismissing from the MUP and what measures were supposed to be taken in similar situations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I apologise. I said both the admission and the regularity of their conduct.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, you should be clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is this document about, as a matter of fact?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: This document is both an instruction and an order as to how to deal with members of the MUP who have committed some of the acts contained herein. They should be removed from the ministry and all the legal measures should be undertaken and criminal proceedings should be launched against them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there cases when you had to remove people from the ministry as a result of irregularities in their job performance?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: When we are talking about people being dismissed, we have to make a distinction between reserve policemen and active-duty policemen working in the MUP. When it comes to active-duty policemen working in the MUP, their immediate superior had to file a report to the disciplinary commission and launch disciplinary proceedings before the first-instance disciplinary commission. There were various kinds of measures. The first one was transfer to a new job to dismissal from the MUP. And obviously if there were elements of a crime, a criminal report was filed to the competent prosecutor's office. When it came to reserve police officers working for the MUP who were employed as military reservists who were recruited at the request of the MUP and by the Secretariat for National Defence deployed to work as reserve policemen, together with active-duty police officers, and when those people committed a certain breach of discipline, they would be removed from our records as reserve police officers and the Secretariat for National Defence would receive information about that, and then such individuals would be engaged in military units either as reservists or deployed elsewhere. In case they committed a crime, in addition to being eliminated or removed from the records, criminal proceedings were also instituted against them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your staff members, did they implement that policy?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Before I answer your question, I have to emphasise that the problem with reservists arose even while they -- we were members of the joint Ministry of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The SDA and the HDZ did not allow reserve military to respond to the call-ups of the JNA, but they, rather, redeployed them as members of the MUP. In doing that, they didn't take to account whether they had criminal records, whether there were criminal proceedings instituted against them, or any similar thing. And that was done in the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which means that at the beginning during the time of division, and especially in the war, police stations which were set up by the Crisis Staff, they admitted people without applying any criteria whatsoever. They would employ reservists as members of the MUP. And that is why, in view of the fact in the state of emergency that was declared in Republika Srpska or a state of war, rather, the number of reservists and the -- and active-duty policemen was determined by the president of the state which is regulated by the Law on the Army and All People's Defence. That's why I sent you and the assembly a proposal to disband reserve contingents and that they should be reduced to a reasonable number that would be necessary only for the tasks performed by the Ministry of the Interior. Such decisions were issued by the Presidency and by the Assembly, and then I could keep on insisting, and if my report is precise, and I believe that it is close to precise, on 6.000 people being removed from the records of the Ministry of Interior, those people were reservists on our records up to then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The question remains whether your members of staff implemented your policy, and also can you tell us who Dobro Planojevic was?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Dobro Planojevic was my assistant for crime prevention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he implement the policy that you drafted? Did he implement the policy that you drafted?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: All of my assistants implemented what I requested from them. However, they were not 100 per cent committed to that. And after the first collegium that we held at the time when we could, because there hadn't been any physical contact among us, so we held it in Belgrade, that's where we met, and that's when certain information was shared. I was not informed about that collegium and I invited my assistants to resign from their positions because I had not been very happy with their work in the past.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown D01527.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please pay attention. This was issued on the 5th of June. It says that the assistant for crime prevention -- and if I may remind you that he points to the fact that there were members of the police who -- whose conduct was in inadmissible, and please pay attention to the last sentence where it says: "On this occasion, we would like to draw your attention that in contact vis-a-vis the civilian population and prisoners of war, you should strictly adhere to the rules of the international rules of war." How is that in compliance with what you already told us about the policy in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: This is the result of our meeting -- of the meeting of an inner circle, the under-secretary for public security and the assistant for policing and crime prevention. That's when we talked about this -- this problem precisely and how to carry out an on-site investigation. Dobro Planojevic, as one of the assistants, sent this as an instruction to the people on the ground to show them how they should behave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive anything from the Presidency -- president of the Presidency, i.e., from myself, with regard to the implementation of this policy?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I just stated what the reaction was to the dismantling of war police stations and special detachments that were set up by the Crisis Staffs. They were paramilitary -- paramilitaries, not the police, in accordance with our regulations. Let me not go any further than that. And that helped for my orders to be fully implemented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown 65 ter 25454.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will also see a translation. And you say here on the 27th of July: "In accordance with the order by the president of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," dated 25th and 26th July. Which means on the following day, you issued your own order? My attention is drawn by paragraph 2 where it says that you are invoking your previous order. And you say: "In accordance with my order, strictly confidential number," so-and-so, "of 23rd July, 1992, I hereby order immediately to remove from the Ministry of the Interior individuals who have been held criminally responsible for crimes that are prosecuted ex officio ..." You made exception for political and verbal offences which were also prosecuted ex officio during the Communist reign; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I can explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Stanisic. We are not getting the interpretation. Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, you can see at -- a complete procedure. On the 17th of July, I was in Belgrade at a collegium. That was the first collegium that we could possibly hold. So I drafted a report, and I sent it to the president of the state and the prime minister. Because what I learnt at that collegium made me believe that there were problems that I, as a minister, and my members of staff within the Ministry of Interior could deal with, and that's why I immediately issued my own orders or, rather, conclusions that I wanted to reach every individual on the ground and show them how they should deal with certain matters. What I couldn't deal with with my staff members I thought that it was my obligation to inform the prime minister about that, as well as the president of the state, and urge them to use their authority to issue their own orders to other bodies which could deal with certain problems that I emphasised in my report. I wanted us to act simultaneously in order to prevent all those negative matters that I had been informed about during the collegium meeting. And here, you can see that the president took my report under advisement. You can see that he also reached certain conclusions and sent his orders to the Ministry of the Interior. When it comes to paragraph 2, you can see that already on the 23rd of July, I sent an order to deal with certain issues that pertained to my authorities, and then I again issued my orders after receiving your instruction and sent my information to the people on the grounds.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'd like to see paragraph 7 and 8 on the following page, although the entire document is really worth or entire attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here in paragraph 7 you say: "Make sure to remove from areas where they are active all groups and individuals that are not under the control of the Army of the Serbian Republic, and to collect information about anyone who commits any kind of crime, hand them over to competent institutions and take measures in accordance with the provisions of the Law on Criminal Procedure." Paragraph 8, "I order once again ..." You repeat your own order, therefore. When was that first orders issued? On the 23rd?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was on it's 23rd, as you can see on page 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That all members of the Ministry of the Interior must perform the duties, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Not only that. Please. Since we're looking at this document, I would like to draw your attention to paragraph 6. Not only did I issue my orders in writing but I also tasked particular assistants in various regions to be in charge of implementing that order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in paragraph 6, are we talking about some very experienced personnel?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were my assistants, people who -- who had most experience and who had highest positions in the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4273, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we'll have a break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Excellencies. The document is the document that Minister Stanisic referred to. That's for all the participants in these proceedings. This is instruction and an overview of the work of the Ministry of the Interior. And after that, all the other documents were sent to the Presidency and to the officials on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the document number is D447.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not recorded that the document number is D477, which is the record of the meeting in Belgrade. There is no need for me to show it because it has already been admitted. And now it seems to be okay. 447, with a 7. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for record -- for the record, we would like to express our gratitude to the Registry and the AV booth for providing us with the -- with the LiveNote transcript. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. I'll thank them also. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Minister, as for this removal of people who were not eligible or incapable, this cleansing of such people in the MUP, did you present this to the public? So did people know that it cannot and should not be done that way?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Of course. All the measures that we took were made public, and information could be obtained about all of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what amount of time was needed -- or, actually, what had we inherited in terms of the rule of law? So how much time did we need to get into the saddle, or, rather, if I can put it this way, to introduce the rule of law?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the constitution of an institution largely depends on the conditions involved. The conditions that prevailed in Republika Srpska -- or, rather, in all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I think that we in the Ministry of the Interior made a super-human effort to organise ourselves in order to be able to function and to take measures as envisaged by the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 65 ter 10838.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please help us with this. Tell us what is it that we see here? Did you give this interview to "Javnost" on the 30th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see the middle of the second column. Yes, that would be about it. The upper part, please. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now this is what I'd like that ask you: You say here that I would like to point out that we have a highly responsible attitude towards the members of our service.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not manage to find the passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We didn't hear anything, Mr. Karadzic. Please find the passage first and then let them know where you are reading from.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The cursor was there right now in the Serbian version. Yes. I would like to point out, yes. But, in English -- in English, it should probably be the next page. [In English] I would also like to point out ... [Interpretation] The cursor was there. The lower half of the page: Unfortunately, the ministry and so on forth. Yes, here it is: "I would also like to point out ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you say here that, and further on, you say: "I think that nowadays we are the only ministry, some members of which have been expelled from our ranks not because they did anything against the Serbian interest because they committed individual acts succumbing to base instincts which really does not befit a member of our service." Tell me, what do you mean by this, "the only ministry"? What do you mean, the only Ministry of the Interior in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: No. I wanted to say - and that was the truth - that the position of the ministry was to make a super-human effort to create something and to be among the first ministries of Republika Srpska. In terms of setting up this system of the Ministry of the Interior so that we could, as adequately as possible, and as best possible, protect everything that the police is supposed to protect in the area of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then in the next paragraph, you say --

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Sorry, can I just add something to that. I pointed this out to see that it was quite necessary, especially for the Ministry of Justice and the military judiciary and the military prosecutor's office, to work on this as energetically as possible so that if we processed someone, we, within the Ministry of the Interior, up to the point where as far as we can go, then we would want the other ministries to do what is necessary in terms of their work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see line 4 underneath the photograph. That's in Serbian. And we'll find the reference in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To what extent were crimes uncovered?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, in view of the conditions in which the ministry operated then, and taking into account all the problems that existed in one part, it was rather satisfactory in terms of uncovering crimes even if we look at the situation worldwide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And we say here --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot find this in the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, until October 1992, what was the number of criminal reports involved?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I really would not want to engage in guess-work now. I don't have any exact figures and it's been a long time, and I cannot remember the number of criminal reports or the number of perpetrators. After all, this was done by the crime investigation service and, at the time, I received information from them, and I presented this information that is contained here. Perhaps you can show me something else that I could comment upon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: D447. There is a reference to September, perhaps even earlier than that. Several thousand criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D447.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct that there were several thousand immediately at the very outset?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, irrespective of what figures say, I'm sorry that this percentage was not even higher. Unfortunately, the situation was such that it is reflected in these indicators, regardless of the willingness to do things and everything that we did, indeed, do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On document P261, page 24 in Serbian, it says, that 2500 forensic expertise projects were carried out only in the area of CSB Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We could not follow the figures that are being read out very fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we didn't hear anything. Please read slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P2761 is the document that I'm referring to. We don't need to call it up. The participants can see this. In Serbian, it's page 20, and English 24. There's a reference to thousands, 8.000 on-site investigations. 27.000 interviews in 1992 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the document before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, it's 23 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see this point. Yes, I'll hear from Mr. Zecevic first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I just thought that in all fairness the document should be shown to the witness to comment it, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I was just going to note that this document is not in the statement and not on their list of exhibits, so I was unaware that this document was going to be used by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's a document of his ministry. Or, actually, he had already left, but it speaks about his work too, and there are no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a separate matter, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any objection, Mr. Olmsted?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4274, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, did you do anything, and, if so, what is it that you did do, in relation to possibly credible information about paramilitary elements and independent elements, persons who behaved in a criminal way? Actually, let me narrow this down a bit. Can you tell me what happened in Brcko, Zvornik, Bijeljina, in the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: As far as paramilitary groups are concerned and their crimes or, rather, incriminations of any kind, there are two periods involved. That is to say, up until the collegium, and after the collegium in Belgrade. That is to say, up until the 11th of July, and after the 11th of July. What you mentioned, Brcko, Zvornik, and Bijeljina, this information about possible crimes and their perpetrators, that was before the collegium. Since during a considerable period of time we did not have any communication with this part, and as soon as communication was established, this first information came in about possible criminal behaviour on the part of these paramilitary groups. Since this information was incomplete, it was talk mostly, I specifically charged two persons. I asked an inspector from public security and another inspector from state security to go out into the field and collect more information, which is what they did. And then an assessment was made on the basis of this information, and the assessment was that we did not have the potential to deal with these groups on our own because there were quite a few of them and mostly these were criminal groups that had come from Serbia. And they were linked to criminal groups in the territory of Republika Srpska. I asked you, and you contacted the then-prime minister of - what was it called then? - the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, but along my own line, I also informed the federal minister - I think his name was Petar Gracanin - and I asked that they send us by way of assistance some of their forces, precisely for that reason; namely, that most of these criminal groups were from the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember the names of the persons that you sent to carry out this additional investigation?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Our request was met, and Petar Gracanin sent Mico Davidovic, who held some position in the special brigade of the federal MUP. And he originally hailed from Bijeljina, and he was familiar with the area. And he arrived with a unit of the federal SUP of Yugoslavia. He arrived in Bijeljina. I issued a clear and unequivocal order to him; that is to say, all paramilitary groups that are in that area are to be eliminated and arrested. As for those who had not been committed crimes, they should be expelled; and those who had committed crimes should be prosecuted. And that's, indeed, what was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where these arrests took place? First of all, can you tell us whether the local authorities, the civilian authorities, the police stations, were they capable of doing that without any kind of external assistance?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Not in this area. Our assessment was that even viewed from all of Republika Srpska, we could not handle that. At that time, there was still no communication with the other centres Banja Luka, Doboj, Herzegovina. So there was only the potential that was there in that area, and that is why we asked for this assistance from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us where arrests took place during this operation -- or, rather, first of all, was it only the federal MUP or did you also provide something? Who took part in these arrests?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: A unit of the federal MUP arrived and we also attached a number of personnel, I think it was a platoon of MUP members. Together they were in Brcko, Bijeljina, and partially Zvornik. They put in place conditions for -- for the rule of law to be established in the area, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many were arrested?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened with those who were arrested?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: What followed was the next stage. After it was learned at the collegium meeting in Belgrade that in the municipality of Zvornik, there were two or three paramilitary groups which comprised over 100 men who were exceptionally well armed, I reissued my order to the chief, Dragan Andan, I believe his name was, as well as to Mico Davidovic and to the special brigade of the MUP of the RS headed by Milenko Karisik. However, since it was learned by way of information from the field that the group included members of the VRS, or at least they introduced themselves as such, using VRS IDs, I asked the VRS to send a number of their military policemen to co-operate with us. Unfortunately, under the then-law, the civilian police could not arrest soldiers, and it was for that reason that such co-operation was required. It was, indeed, done, and that is how the group was arrested. There was even some engagement with a number of wounded. In any case, the group was arrested, eliminated, some of them fled during the arrest, and the problem was dealt with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did those who were arrested in Zvornik end up?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: The MUP submitted criminal reports and notified the competent prosecutor's office and the competent court in Bijeljina, and together, in co-operation with Serbia, or the former SFRY, since there were a number of Serbian citizens, Serbian nationals, they took measures together, which we did not take part in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a specific reason why you handed it over to the Serbian judiciary?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: The judicial system on our side was in its inception, and we did not have adequate courts which could try them. I'd rather not go into speculating what was agreed upon between the two sides though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any information on the paramilitaries and crimes in Podrinje, Visegrad and Rudo? And according to the information you had, who was responsible for it?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just wanted to add something to the previous part. In terms of what I know, and regarding that part of the country, it was the military security took responsibility of the person who was at the time suspected of having killed some 200 people in the environs of Zvornik. It fell under the competence of the military security service and the military prosecutor's office. As for the rest who were suspected of having committed more simple crimes, such as theft, they were transmitted to the Ministry of the Interior. That is what I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that we are back on that topic, do you know whether the state of Serbia ever completed its proceedings against them?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I know they processed some of them, although I have no further information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now go back to the issue of Podrinje, Rudo and Visegrad. Did you have any other information regarding it and did the ministry do anything?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: After this operation, the next day, I arrived in Zvornik. I called a meeting with the people who participated in the operations, and I ordered the following: Similar operation against any paramilitary or parapolice groups were to be continued. And I was very clear and unambiguous on that point. I told them that it had to be done even at the risk of their own lives. We had information that in parts of Rudo and Visegrad, there were also some paramilitary organisations which were active. I ordered that a platoon be established immediately of some 30 personnel, members of the MUP, in order to execute that task. We had a problem though. Due to interrupted communications, the only way for us to reach Visegrad was via the FRY. A dispatch was sent to the FRY, asking that a -- transport be allowed for the unit with the necessary weapons and equipment they needed through their territory in order to reach Rudo and Visegrad. Of course, since the FRY also had UN observers in its territory, they did not allow the unit to move in that way. Therefore, there was some time lost. In any case, ultimately, the unit was transferred and continued its work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I move on, can you tell us which category of the population, ethnically and socially speaking, was exposed the most to the activity of those groups in Rudo, Zvornik, and Visegrad? Which was the most vulnerable group that you were trying to protect?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, whoever seen as an obstacle to a criminal group becomes their target, but in this case they particularly targeted non-Serbs. They wanted to gain -- to achieve material gain. I apologise. They did not shy from committing mass crimes in order to achieve that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To achieve what?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Their goals of gaining material benefit, to steal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That something prompted you particularly to have the unit sent to Visegrad and Rudo?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I told you that we had information that some 20 people were kidnapped in a certain location, and the presence of paramilitary organisations and volunteers was established. They did so in conjunction with domestic criminals all over the territory of Rudo and Visegrad. Thus, the unit was sent to engage them and to secure normal living conditions in the area, to the extent possible. You know that throughout the war Visegrad itself or its environs were subjected to combat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown 1D09511.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this is.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: This represents the implementation of my order. You see that my name is in the signature block. It was drafted by Milos Duban [phoen], the chief of police working for the MUP of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be reflected in the transcript that the document concerns Minister Mico Stanisic. I don't see the name on the first page, but I believe -- yes, in the English translation we have it on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the unit you referred to a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4275, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Minister, you said you did not make any distinction. Can you tell us what happened when Serbs committed crimes against non-Serbs, i.e., Muslims and Croats? What kind of procedure followed?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. Can you reformulate, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the conduct of the law enforcement agencies, including the ministry, because you can certainly speak on its behalf?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior acted in accordance with the instructions and orders. It treated equally all perpetrators, especially when it came to serious crime. If I may, I'd like to clarify something. What was the problem for the Ministry of the Interior in terms of arresting the perpetrators when crimes were committed against Muslims? Such crimes usually took place at demarcation lines where there was combat. In that case, the victims and witnesses went to the Muslim side, and we were in no position to interview them, to gather the necessary information about the perpetrators. You know well what kind of solidarity exists among such perpetrators who commit such crimes. So we were unable to reach the witnesses, and there was much problem in gathering information. That is why we issued the order from June, that at least the necessary evidence be gathered. I was the minister of the interior. My colleagues, at the time we were discussing it, told me, if we arrest anyone without proof we would have to release them immediately. So the precondition was to gather evidence, and only then suspects could be brought in and procedure initiated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness briefly be shown D449.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall this letter of yours sent to the prime minister?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can I see the signature block? Is this the original letter by me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we both -- can we have both versions, the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's a stay on this page. You said something a moment ago. I will read it out: We are working on gathering and documenting the crimes of murder -- of war crimes of murder and genocide irrespective of the ethnicity of the perpetrators. The date of this letter is the 18th of July, 1992. Does it tally with what the ministry was doing at the time?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: You know we had the problem with the paramilitary groups and the problem was caused by Ms. Plavsic. She even sent letters to the Cossacks, to Draskovic, and Arkan to sort of send their volunteers to help the defence of the Serbian people in Republika Srpska. All those who came, for the most part, were people prone to committing crimes with prior convictions, for similar crimes. This is why when I returned from the collegium meeting in Belgrade, since I had insisted from the start to dealing lawfully with the issue of volunteer and until when a person can be a volunteer, because it happened that such groups, which she invited, reported to certain units, they were issued with arms, they would introduce themselves as some kind of special forces, and they would get the best weapons, and then they would take off and commit crimes. Having obtained their initial status as part of the military, they excluded the competence of the minister of the interior because, then they fell under the jurisdiction of the military security service, the military prosecutor, and the military courts; whereas, as a matter of fact, there were not with the army. They were simply committing crimes in the rear. It was probably due to the pressure put by Ms. Plavsic to presenting them as her forces, and in order not to have them prosecuted such things never found its way on any agenda. Thus, I was forced to act the way I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's correct line 7, page 75, the witness said they joined the military. They actually excluded themselves from the competency of the ministry, of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you agree with it, Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. The affiliation with the military actually excluded them from the competence of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can see that as early as July you issued documents to that effect. When you had witnesses and victims to perform investigation, what happened?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: It depended. There was such cases in our territory during the war where witnesses could be obtained, but most of them were absent. They were interviewed in the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the Muslim part, but those statements were never made available to us. On the other hand, we were not members of the Interpol so we did not have any ways to seek that documentation or information about the crimes. We were still not recognised as a state.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D09505. This should not be broadcast because it contains victim names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Minister, don't mention any names, but can you please tell us what this document is about? And also can you tell us whether there was a trial and when could it have taken place?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I can only tell you what I read. This was not within my jurisdiction. I didn't have anything whatsoever to do with individual reports. However, you can read in the document that the crime was committed on the 25th of May, 1992, that a criminal report was filed subsequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 26th; right?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: There is a number here, 25th of May, this is what I'm reading.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, the date of the document is 26 May.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about the incident, however. And there's also the date of 26th of May, 1993, when the file was reported.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The crime was rape. What is the rapist's ethnic background? We don't have to mention his name.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Judging by the name, he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where from? Where did he reside?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: He was from Pancevo, in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness has already said that this was not within his jurisdiction. He didn't have anything whatsoever to do with this individual report, and now Mr. Karadzic is simply reading parts of it and having the witness confirm that that's what the document says. This is of no value to this case, and therefore we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I tend to agree with Mr. Olmsted's observation. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic, with respect this document, after having heard witness's answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Minister, how did this end up with the district court in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Could you please show me the page where -- with the signature block? I would like to see who it is who filed the criminal report, whether it was the Ministry of the Interior. Maybe then I would be able to tell you something more about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us see how it goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have the name of the prosecutor here, the deputy public prosecutor that is. As a rule, who is it who is in charge of investigations and handing the matter over to the prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I've already described in great detail about the procedure, the investigation, and on-site inspections, and so on and so forth. However, that doesn't mean that if the Ministry of the Interior cannot collect evidence on -- on a crime, and if they do so, they can file a criminal report to the prosecutor's office irrespective of any on-site inspection. This could have been sent from the Ministry of the Interior to the prosecutor's office at that time because the perpetrator was a civilian and the civilian prosecutor's office would have been in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now could you please tell us where it says in paragraph 4 that an official of the SJB Bratunac should be heard because they prevented the perpetrators from raping the women. So it was just attempted ripe; right?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm reading. This is what I can read under paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that member of the SJB an employee of your ministry?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: If he was a policeman in a police station then he was also a member of the Ministry of the Interior; right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And now can we go back to page 1. Let's not mention any names. Who was the victim, in terms of her ethnic background? What was her ethnic background? And I'm still talking about this attempted rape.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Can we go back one page. Judging by her name, the victim was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be admitted? It obviously points to the fact that the document reached the prosecutor's office via the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Regardless of what the document says, Mr. Karadzic has not shown a nexus between this document and this witness. This witness is simply reiterating what the document itself says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I would submit that this document is admissible because it is consistent with his testimony of how these matters were handled and that prosecutions and investigations were carried out for crimes against non-Serbs committed by Serbs. And following our practice, that's sufficient for the document to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add to that, your Excellencies, none of us high officials are charged with anything that they may have done. We are all charged with the conduct of our subordinates. And here you can see that Mr. Stanisic's subordinates actually did everything by the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are not a minister at this time, Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a minister when the crime was committed and when the criminal report was submitted to the competent public prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, are you saying you are aware that a criminal report was sent to the public prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in view of my position and the scope of my tasks, I can only state that a member of the Ministry of the Interior, i.e., of the Bratunac police station, submitted this criminal report to the public prosecutor and that the prosecutor's office took the matter over. I did not look at all the individual reports because it was not my duty. So I really can't remember this particular report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The incident happened on the 25th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And at that time, I was a minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4276, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think we need to put it under seal. Just for the -- out of abundance of caution, Mr. Karadzic didn't want to read out the name of the victim and sexual harassment. But I don't think we should admit it under seal. Do you have any observation, Mr. Olmsted?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, I think we can provide a redacted version of this so that the name of the victim doesn't appear in the public record. Since it is not an essential part of this testimony, I think it would be a more prudent way to do that. Even though the exhibit's not broadcast, members of the public have access to the exhibits, and I don't see the need to identify a victim of a sexual crime without some good reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it mean that you are tendering two versions of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we have no difficulty with it. Shall we assign numbers for those.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The public redacted version will be Exhibit D4277.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now I'd like to show 1D09506.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have just told us that at the time of the commission of this crime, documents were gathered, evidence was collected, but that it was not always possible to carry out trials during the war? Now look at this judgement. It was passed in 1993. I would like to look at page 4. Please look at the ethnic background of the victim and also the ethnic background of the perpetrator. Karadzic is the perpetrator and the victim is Ramic.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Judging by the names, the perpetrator was a Serb and the victim was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at Serbian 4 and English 2, and then we will move onto page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pay attention to the lower part of this page where it says in the evidentiary procedure, on the consensual recommendation of the parties, the court read out the following: The statements given by the interviewed, and the witness, Husein Ramic, Emina Ramic, Enver Ramic and Selim Cajic, and the psychiatric expert report by neuropsychiatrist Dr. Bojan Stojakovic of 30 July, 2001, excerpts from the Sipovo SJB criminal records for the accused, the medical documentation, the report and external examination of the body. Okay, what did the MUP do when the crime was committed? They examined the body. They did the expert analysis of the weapons. Did they do everything that was in their power for a trial to be conducted at some point?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was an on-site inspection by the Ministry of the Interior. There was a crime technician who was involved. All the evidence was gathered. And eventually the Trial Judgement was founded on the evidence gathered at the time when the crime was committed. And the evidence was irrefutable and it was the grounds for the judgement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said irrefutable evidence on which the judgement was founded. Can the document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would object on several grounds. First of all, this is a judgement not from 1993 but from 2003. It involves -- well, purportedly involves a crime that occurred in Sipovo, which, as I understand it, is not part of the indictment in this case. And although it appears that some work was done on this case, it doesn't say when that work was done by the police. It just says that there was some examination of a fire-arm, et cetera. And once again, this witness has no personal knowledge of this case. He's simply reciting what the document itself states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The last page, which we are seeing now, refers to the criminal records of 2nd of February, 1993, as well as on-site investigation on 10th of September, 1992. As such, we have a basis to admit it, don't we? I will consult my colleagues. Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4278, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we not have to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- have a redacted version or not? I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a homicide and the first was a failed rape attempt. Both judgements are in the public domain already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another document please, 09507.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is another judgement. Could you please tell us about the ethnicity of the perpetrators of those crimes.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Judging by the names, one could conclude that they are Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the preamble, it says the district court in Banja Luka in chamber composed of so-and-so, in the criminal case against the accused so-and-so, for war crimes against civilians under article so-and-so, and so on and so forth. Further down there is reference to everything that had been done.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we go to English 4 and Serbian 3. English 3; Serbian 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's see what the MUP did at the time. It says when it comes to the physical evidence, the public prosecutor's office presented to the Trial Chamber the following evidence: The record of the external examination of the body; an Official Note drafted by the Bosanski Novi public security station, dated 22nd, which was also the on-site investigation report; the minutes, and so on and so forth. Did the MUP undertake all the actions that eventually led to this judgement?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: It is obvious it is evident that the judgement was passed based on the evidence that was collected in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to the following pages in both languages. At the very top, the following says that defence also presented evidence by presenting the schematic of the house in Novi Grad that was drafted by Mirko Karlica. Now, when it comes to forensic technician, who do they belong to?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: They belong to the crime prevention services of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Maybe it be noted that the interpreters cannot find these passages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dated 22nd in respect of the aforementioned schematic where it is recorded that charred bodies and their remains were found on site. On the 21st of October with -- Muslim witnesses were interviewed as you can see in the last sentence of the paragraph. The Bosanski Novi CS -- CJB took statements by Bakira, Kasim, and Djulka; right?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: This is precisely what I was talking about. Whenever we had occasion to locate witnesses, obviously crime prevention inspector and members of the Novi Grad police station acted extremely professionally and when they carried out on-site inspection and when they interviewed witnesses, the procedure was the same. However, the problem was that by and large we could not get access to any of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the ethnicity of these witnesses is?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: It is obviously on the basis of their names and surnames that they are Muslims. You see, she gave quite a bit of information. She knows them as neighbours. That is what was missing, in order for more light to be shed on the perpetrators. Information was collected about each and every crime. I don't know of any omissions there. But as for perpetrators, it was hard to collect information. It was hard to be in this situation as stated here. Namely that witnesses were on the spot, or rather, that they were accessible to the Ministry of the Interior and since that is what the situation was, I believe that they acted quite properly here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this please be admitted, this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it for the same reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you identify the relevant pages -- pages, that is, matching with English translation. We'll admit only those part.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4279, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it's the first and second and third and fourth, fifth, and sixth -- no. Fifth, in Serbian, and up to page 4 in English. The first four in English ; and the first five in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Minister, when you were explaining why perpetrators who hailed from Serbia were handed over to Serbia, you said that there weren't enough courts of law. Can you tell us how the civilian and military judiciary was established? Actually, the result of the work of the Ministry of the Interior depended on the civilian judiciary. So what did this look like, and when could one count on expeditiousness?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I think it was only in mid-June that decisions were made to establish courts of law, and then people were actually being appointed. There was really a shortage of people, people who were trained and capable of being prosecutors and judges. Also, for example, a prosecutor's office would be established, but there wouldn't be a prosecutor there. There would be only be a secretary who would be receiving documents; for instance, they would write 1992 and the prosecutor would actually start operating in 1993 and even later. So those were the problems involved. It was hard to constitute this kind of institution overnight. These problems were of a substantive nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: And that was the main problem in terms of passing judgements and finally bring before justice at least those perpetrators that we had arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me whether I or somebody relevant from the leadership of Republika Srpska asked you at any point in time not to have crimes investigated, crimes committed by Serbs, especially against non-Serbs, Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: You did not ask me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we have a language problem here with prisoners and captives. Tell me, prisoners of war, under whose authority did they fall and what is the difference between a prisoner of war and a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we have three concepts: Prisoners of war is solely under the military and has to do with the military. Detainees can be persons who are detained in military prisons and in civilian prisons. And there is yet another category, whereby the Ministry of the Interior can keep a person in custody for up to three days when there are reasons for that. However, a decision has to be made to that effect. And the public prosecutor has to be informed or an investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how could a detainee be kept longer? On which basis?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "longer"? I don't understand. You have to be very specific there. Which category?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Longer than what you said about police custody.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Regardless of whether it's a civilian or military prison, a detainee can be in prison only within the sentence passed. That is as far as prisoners are concerned. Now, as for detainees, that decision is made by a judge up to six months, according to the law that was in force then. It was for shorter terms but then these shorter terms could be extended, as far as I can remember. It wasn't really my line of work. So I'm speaking on the basis of memory now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it allowed and did you take any measures against the abuse of the institute of detention that was not based on regulations?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Whenever I heard any such thing, I said that measures should be taken. And that was unequivocal. And you can see that for my orders.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D467. Could that please be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, Minister, this order of yours? It says in the second line, "I hereby order ...," the 10th of August, 1992. Tell us what is prescribed in this order?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Number 1: "Detention and holding measures shall be applied exclusively within existing regulations." That's what I talked about a moment ago. You should be personally responsible for the lives of people who are being held and detained and for preventing any form of abuse in that area. The premises where people are being held or detained must fulfil basic hygiene and health requirements." Now 2: "The security of collection centres shall be directly responsible of the Serbian army and, if they do not have enough personnel for these duties, it shall therefore be necessary to engage members of the reserve police for these tasks and to place them at the army's disposition." My understanding was that a member of the Ministry of the Interior cannot carry out such duties because this is detention that is under the military, and we cannot exercise control and it is for that reason that I issued this kind of order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So a reservist of the police, is such a person at the same time a military reservist and if this person does something for the military, does such a person has to be under its command?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the beginning of the answer. There was no pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could repeat your answer. Because of the overlap, interpreters were not able to hear you, Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Members of the military reserve are part of the records of the Secretary for National Defence. As for the work done by the Ministry of the Interior, if they need reenforcements at the proposal of authorised officials from the ministry, persons who are reserve soldiers can be sent but this is the Secretary for National Defence that decides. The Ministry of the Interior has to train such a person, if this does happen, so that such a person could try to do a good job when engaged as a reservist in the work of the Ministry of the Interior. When this is no longer necessary within the Ministry of the Interior, then such a person would be returned to the Secretariat of National Defence, again, to be -- in their records and to be used for the needs of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We see here in the first paragraph that you underline the question of hygiene; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we briefly take look at 269 -- sorry, D469. A week later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is also yours. "I hereby order yet again," that's what you say. And then also you are referring to informal prisons, unofficial prisons, also to have improper behaviour sanctioned. And you also say in paragraph 3: "As for persons who violate valid regulations and act in contravention of our laws and international provisions, in this area, regardless of whether they are civilians or members of the MUP or the military, it is necessary to collect information and documentation for submitting criminal reports to the appropriate prosecutor's office?"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: This was the end of the sight translation and we did not hear the question or the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The witness -- the interpreters did not hear your question and answer. Repeat your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question was: Who this was sent to, this order, a week later.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: To all chiefs of centres in Republika Srpska. However, Your Honours, may I just explain this term "unofficial" or "informal" so there's no misunderstanding. I meant any kind of detention apart from detention that is regulated on the basis of legal provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I must say that I omitted to say that in the Serbian version the word "divlji" is under quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for myself, as president to the Presidency, did you get any written communication from me? And how did they fit into your own efforts and the positions that you took?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: They were complementary to the orders that I sent, whatever I received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 16257. Could that please be shown to the witness. That's the 65 ter number. 16257. That's the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember this letter, and can you tell us who it is that is sending it, and to who, and what such a person is asking for? You don't have to read it out.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: I have to read it to myself. How could I remember all of this? Yes, I did receive this, just like all the other addressees. You say here, in terms of the authority that everyone had, we should all do our best to allow access to the International Red Cross and you sent this to the Ministry of Justice and to the MUP and to the army. And we acted on that basis, since the prisons are under the Ministry of Justice, the camps are under the military, and our obligation was to secure transit to the facility that the -- the representatives of the International Red Cross wanted to go to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D103. That is the number under which this was already admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know on the whole and in detail what my position was in terms of humane treatment, an observance of international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, on the basis of what I knew, on the basis of your communication to me and also it was translated into my own orders, that is what I know. What I know is translated into these orders. As for more than that, well, after all, you were the president. It was not within my domain to know everything about you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Minister, could you please tell us now what it was that you knew and when you found out and how about a crime that was committed at Koricanske Stijene on the 21st of August, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I will have to object at this point and ask the Trial Chamber if it insists on the answer and to compel the witness to answer on that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- if the parties like to make any observation as to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We would ask the Trial Chamber to compel him to answer this question.
